What I do think is interesting is your claim that "economics is based on classical mathematics", which I rather think is ostensibly false, though I can understand how you might have concluded this if you haven't done much economics. In my own university there are development economists and Marxian economists whose work owes little to mathematics of any kind. In this they follow in traditions that go back to Proudhon. Indeed, there are Green economists and feminist economists who would explicitly disavow mathematical approaches. The problem is that all these approaches/schools are what we might call "heterodox economics", which means that they tend not to be taught at undergraduate level in many schools.

What makes your claim interesting is that although it's easy to produce ostensible counterexamples (as I've just done) it's also possible to interpret your remark as meaning "economics is based on underlying logic all of which can be captured within classical mathematics". This is not immediately obvious, and although I have a sense that it's probably true I'd probably want to see rather more substance to this claim than bland assertion. Can we take green economics and mathematize it, for example? At first sight it might be difficult to do this, as at least some green economists reject quantifying some economic variables, but do they still (for example) impose preference orders? If they do, can we map these to (e.g.) posets (a sort of algebraic structure) and thus import that body of abstract algebra into economics? This is not a trivial topic, and I don't know the answer. It's certainly a question worth asking, though, and might make a nice project for someone.
